question: What is the main job of a mechanical ventilator in the hospital?

options.A: To assist or replace spontaneous breathing and maintain gas exchange
options.B: To deliver high-dose aerosolized antibiotics directly to the lungs
options.C: To permanently replace the function of damaged lung alveoli
options.D: To cure underlying pulmonary infections and lung tissue damage

explanation: You've got this! Mechanical ventilators simply step in to do the work of breathing when a patient's body is too weak to manage oxygen on its own. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h1)

question: Why would a patient with a severe drug overdose and low consciousness urgently need a mechanical ventilator?
explanation: Spot on! When someone is deeply unconscious, they lose reflexes like coughing and swallowing, meaning they could easily inhale stomach contents into their lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h1)

question: Which ventilator mode takes over completely, giving a set rate and volume without letting the patient take spontaneous breaths?
explanation: Great try! Controlled Mandatory Ventilation (CMV) handles the entire breathing cycle for the patient without waiting for them to trigger a breath. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h2)

question: What is the main reason for adding pressure support to a patient who is already breathing on their own through a ventilator?

options.A: To paralyze the respiratory muscles during painful procedures
options.B: To help overcome the resistance of the artificial airway
options.C: To completely take over the work of breathing for the patient
options.D: To measure the exact lung compliance of the patient

explanation: Breathing through a narrow plastic tube is tough work! Pressure support gives a gentle push to make it easier for the patient to draw air through the tube. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h2)

question: In ventilator settings, what does the acronym PEEP stand for?
explanation: PEEP keeps a tiny bit of pressure in the tiny air sacs (alveoli) at the very end of a breath so they don't collapse on themselves. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h3)

question: A patient has an ideal body weight of 70 kg. Which tidal volume setting falls within the safe lung-protective range?
explanation: Protective ventilation uses 6 to 8 mL per kg. For a 70 kg patient, that's roughly 420 to 560 mL, making 450 mL a safe and correct choice! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h3)

question: The high-pressure alarm starts beeping loudly on the ventilator. As a nurse, what is a very common cause to check first?

options.A: An accidental extubation of the endotracheal tube
options.B: A deflation of the endotracheal tube cuff
options.C: A loose connection between the tubing and the patient
options.D: Secretions or mucus plug in the endotracheal tube

explanation: Think of it like a blocked straw—if mucus or a kink blocks the tube, the machine has to push harder to get air in, triggering that high-pressure alarm! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h4)

question: Which bedside check gives immediate confirmation that an endotracheal tube is correctly placed in the trachea?

options.D: Arterial blood gas analysis drawn after 30 minutes

explanation: ETCO2 detectors quickly show exhaled carbon dioxide right at the bedside, proving the tube went down the windpipe and not the stomach. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h4)

question: What is the recommended safe pressure range for an endotracheal tube cuff?
explanation: Keeping the cuff pressure between 20 and 30 cmH2O seals the airway nicely without squeezing the delicate blood vessels in the windpipe too hard. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h5)

question: Why should nurses avoid routine, scheduled suctioning of a breathing tube when the patient doesn't actually need it?

options.A: It increases the risk of accidental tube decannulation
options.B: It automatically changes the prescribed ventilator tidal volume
options.C: It can cause mucosal trauma, bleeding, and low oxygen levels
options.D: It causes the ventilator to trigger persistent low-pressure alarms

explanation: Suctioning is helpful when there's mucus, but doing it too often irritates the airway lining and robs the lungs of precious oxygen. Only suction when necessary! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h5)

question: Why is keeping the head of a ventilated patient's bed elevated at 30 to 45 degrees such an important nursing action?
explanation: Gravity is our friend here! Elevating the bed stops oral and stomach fluids from pooling above the tube cuff and trickling down into the lungs to cause pneumonia. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a mechanical complication caused by high pressure settings on a ventilator?
explanation: Spot on! Pneumonia is an infection caused by germs, whereas things like a collapsed lung (pneumothorax) happen from high pressure popping the delicate air sacs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h6)

question: What is the main goal of doing a Spontaneous Breathing Trial (SBT)?

options.A: To measure the exact lung compliance and resistance parameters
options.B: To evaluate if a patient can tolerate breathing without ventilator support
options.C: To allow the patient to recover from heavy sedative medications
options.D: To clear thick mucus plugs from the lower airways before extubation

explanation: An SBT is like a test drive! We lower the machine's help to see if the patient's lungs and muscles are strong enough to handle breathing all on their own. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h7)

question: A patient was just extubated 20 minutes ago and now has a high-pitched whistling sound when breathing in. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Immediate accumulation of secretions in the left main bronchus
options.B: Sudden tension pneumothorax from previous positive pressure
options.D: Laryngeal edema causing partial upper airway obstruction

explanation: That high-pitched sound (stridor) usually means the voice box (larynx) got a little swollen and angry from having the breathing tube resting in it. Good catch! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h7)
